notes: Take after completing the in-class JavaScript Essentials activity (Nov 5).

questions.explanation: `===` is strict equality and does no type conversion, so the number `5` and the string `"5"` are not equal. `==` is loose equality and converts types, so `0 == false` is `true`. Prefer `===`.

options: It prints `HI`, because JavaScript hoists all functions
It throws an error, because `shout` is used before it is defined
questions.explanation: Function declarations (`function greet() {}`) are hoisted, so they can be called before they appear in the file. Arrow functions assigned to a `const` are not, so calling `shout` first throws a `ReferenceError`.

questions.question: Which expressions are `true` only when `n` is divisible by both 3 and 5? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: `%` gives the remainder, so `n % 3 === 0 && n % 5 === 0` checks both conditions directly, and `n % 15 === 0` is equivalent because a number divisible by both 3 and 5 is divisible by 15. The `||` version is true if *either* divides evenly. The `/` version uses division, not remainder, so it is only true when `n` is 0.

options: `Hey Jude by The Beatles`, then `${title} by ${artist}`
`${title} by ${artist}`, then `Hey Jude by The Beatles`
questions.explanation: Only backticks create a template literal that evaluates `${...}`. Text in single or double quotes is a plain string, so the `${...}` is printed as-is.

questions.question: You want `formatDuration(125)` to return `"2:05"`. Which body is correct?
questions.explanation: `Math.floor` rounds the minutes down, `%` gives the leftover seconds, and `padStart` pads the string with a leading zero. `padStart` is a *string* method, so the number must be converted with `String(...)` first (option 3 throws an error). Options 1 and 4 give `2.0833...:5` and `2:5`.

questions.question: Which of these is equivalent to `function double(n) { return n * 2; }`?
questions.explanation: An arrow function with no braces returns the expression automatically (an *implicit return*). With braces you have to write `return` yourself, so option 1 returns `undefined`. The `=>` goes after the parameters.

questions.question: You want an arrow function that returns an object with a `title` property. Which one works?
questions.explanation: JavaScript reads `{` right after `=>` as the start of a function body, not an object. Wrapping the object in parentheses tells JavaScript it's an expression to return.
Spread (`...song`) copies every property into a new object, and the properties listed after it override the copied ones. The original `song` is not changed.

options: A `TypeError`, because the function has two parameters
questions.explanation: The curly braces in the parameter list *destructure* the single object argument, pulling out `title` and `artist` by name. Extra properties (like `year`) are ignored. React uses this pattern for props.
`filter` returns a new array of *every* item that passes the test. `find` returns only the *first* matching item itself (not an array), or `undefined` if nothing matches.

options: It throws an error, because `nums` is a `const`
questions.explanation: `map` returns a *new* array and leaves the original untouched. Because the result wasn't saved in a variable, it was thrown away. Not changing the original is what lets React tell when your data has changed.

questions.question:
Given this code, which line gets the titles of only the songs shorter than 200 seconds?

```javascript
const songs = [
    { title: "Hey Jude", seconds: 431 },
    { title: "Yesterday", seconds: 125 },
    { title: "Respect", seconds: 147 },
];
```
questions.explanation: First `filter` keeps the song objects that are short enough, then `map` pulls the `title` out of each one. In option 4, `map` has already turned the songs into strings, so `s.seconds` is `undefined`. In option 3, `find` returns a single object, which has no `map` method.
A *default* export is imported without braces, using any name you like. *Named* exports are imported in braces using their exact names. A file can have many named exports but only one default export.

options: `response.json()` also returns a promise, so it needs `await`
Nothing, `fetch` already returns the parsed data

`await` can't be used inside an `async` function
questions.explanation: Reading the body takes time too, so `response.json()` returns a promise. Without `await`, `data` is a promise and `data.name` is `undefined`. Write `const data = await response.json();`.

options: An array of title strings, ready to use immediately
A promise that resolves to an array of title strings
A promise that resolves to an array of todo objects
questions.explanation: An `async` function always returns a promise. To use the array, you need `await getTodoTitles(1)` (inside another async function) or `getTodoTitles(1).then((titles) => ...)`. The `map` turns each todo object into its title string.
